# Interior-ocean carbon accumulates faster than tracer ages predict in the upper ocean: a sample-matched test of transit-time anthropogenic CO₂ rates against fifty years of GLODAP DIC

*Draft manuscript — research/dev branch, 2026-11-04. All numbers are generated by code in `research/` (see `research_docs/EXPERIMENT_LOG.md`). Not yet reviewed by a domain expert; references tagged [M] in `REFERENCES.bib` are unverified.*

## Abstract
See `ABSTRACT.md`.

**Keywords:** anthropogenic carbon; dissolved inorganic carbon; GLODAP; transit time distribution; TRACE; eMLR(C*); neutral density; empirical carbon models; validation

---

## 1. Introduction

The ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of anthropogenic CO₂ emissions, and the interior storage of this anthropogenic carbon (C_ant) is the most direct observational constraint on the sink (Sabine et al., 2004; Gruber et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2023). Because C_ant is chemically indistinguishable from natural dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), it is never measured directly. Two families of methods infer it. *DIC-based* methods separate C_ant from repeated DIC measurements using regressions on hydrographic properties (eMLR, eMLR(C*); Friis et al., 2005; Clement & Gruber, 2018). *Tracer-based* methods infer the age distribution of water from transient tracers (CFCs, SF₆) and combine it with the atmospheric CO₂ history under an assumption of steady circulation (transit-time distribution, TTD; e.g., Steinfeldt et al., 2024). The recently released TRACE (Carter et al., 2025) makes TTD-based C_ant available for any sample from its position, temperature, salinity and date, and is *not* trained on DIC.

Where the two families disagree, the disagreement is informative: it indicates either a bias in one method or a real change in natural carbon or circulation that violates the steady-state assumption of TTDs (Gruber et al., 2019; Müller et al., 2023; Steinfeldt et al., 2024). Existing comparisons are made at the level of gridded inventories and decadal differences. To our knowledge, no study has applied *one identical estimator* to observed DIC and to TTD-predicted C_ant at the *same samples* over the full GLODAP record.

This study grew out of an audit of an existing empirical-regression project in this repository, which modelled DIC as a static function of salinity, temperature and apparent oxygen utilisation (AOU) and validated it on later years. We found that its temporal-holdout errors contain a systematic, depth-structured positive drift — the signature expected from anthropogenic carbon uptake. Here we turn this confounder into the object of study and ask:

> Within fixed locations and at fixed (θ, S, AOU), is the observed rate of DIC change, by basin and neutral-density layer, consistent with the rate of C_ant accumulation predicted by TRACE at the same samples?

We also quantify how ignoring this trend affects the validation and selection of static empirical DIC models.

## 2. Data

**GLODAPv2.2023.** We use the merged master file of GLODAPv2.2023 (Lauvset et al., 2024; NOAA NCEI accession 0283442; SHA-256 `002881fa…8766`). Strict quality control retains samples with WOCE flag 2 and secondary-QC flag 1 for DIC, salinity and oxygen, and finite potential temperature, pressure and neutral density γⁿ (428,264 samples). Calculated DIC values (flag 0) and DIC from cruises without secondary QC are excluded; a relaxed, range-only QC (512,384 samples) is used as an ablation.

**Domain.** Atlantic, Indian and Pacific (GLODAP regions 1, 16, 8; north of 35°S) and the Southern Ocean (south of 35°S); Arctic excluded. Nine neutral-density layers with edges at γⁿ = 26.0, 26.5, 27.0, 27.5, 27.8, 28.0, 28.1, 28.2 kg m⁻³. Samples are grouped in 4°×4° cells; only cells whose observations span ≥10 years enter the trend analysis. After inclusion rules the analysis uses **342,277 samples from 515 cruises (1972–2021), in 5,865 cell × layer units across 34 basin × layer groups** (Fig. 1).

**TRACE.** TRACE-Python (Sandborn et al., 2026; release v1.1.2) was evaluated at every sample (historical atmospheric CO₂ trajectory, default disequilibrium; 400,755 of 402,747 strict-QC samples returned finite values).

**eMLR(C*).** The 1° gridded ΔC_ant between 1994 and 2007 of Gruber et al. (2019) (NCEI accession 0186034; standard case and 14-member ensemble).

## 3. Methods

### 3.1 Within-cell trend estimator
For each basin b and layer ℓ we fit

  y_i = α_c(i) + f(θ_i, S_i, AOU_i) + β·(t_i − 2000) + ε_i,

where α_c are cell fixed effects (identifying the trend from repeat sampling of the same cell, which removes changes in where cruises sampled), f is a full quadratic in standardised θ, S and AOU (conditioning on water properties and on respiration), and t is decimal year. The model is fitted by OLS after within-cell demeaning. It is applied with y = observed DIC (β_DIC) and, at the same samples, with y = TRACE C_ant (β_Cant). Because TRACE C_ant depends on T and S, applying the identical estimator yields a like-for-like rate at fixed properties. Estimands are δ = β_DIC − β_Cant and R = β_DIC/β_Cant.

### 3.2 Uncertainty
Confidence intervals come from a cruise-cluster bootstrap (B = 500; cruises resampled with replacement, preserving duplicate draws), joint for DIC and C_ant. A synthetic-recovery experiment (§4.1) calibrated this procedure. We also report an *offset-equivalent detection limit*, 4 µmol kg⁻¹ divided by the median within-cell time span (0.16–0.19 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹): a cumulative systematic DIC offset at the level of GLODAP's adjustment threshold could produce a spurious trend of this size.

### 3.3 Pre-registration and decision rules
Hypotheses, estimators and decision rules were written before the main experiments (`research_docs/RESEARCH_METHODOLOGY.md`). **H1:** in layers with γⁿ ≤ 27.8, R is consistent with 1 — supported if the 95 % CI of R overlaps [0.85, 1.15] (TRACE's ±15 % structural uncertainty). **H2:** deviations concentrate in the Southern Ocean and subpolar North Atlantic (descriptive). **H3:** a time or C_ant covariate removes ≥70 % of the temporal-holdout bias of static DIC regressions. **H4:** deep-layer trends are sensitive to QC (strict vs relaxed). Deviations from the protocol are logged (coverage follow-up; B = 300 for sensitivity runs; the eMLR comparison was added with a decision rule fixed before computation).

### 3.4 Sensitivity analyses
Relaxed QC; cell size 2°, 6°, 8°; minimum span 5 and 15 years; linear conditioning; conditioning without AOU, without θ and S, or with phosphate instead of AOU; post-1990 data only; seasonal harmonics; leave-one-cruise-out; and an unconditioned baseline.

### 3.5 Static empirical models (H3)
We re-implemented the repository's model hierarchy (mean, linear, rank-1 quadratic, rank-2 quadratic, full quadratic, cubic in S, T and AOU) and evaluated each per basin with and without a linear time term or TRACE C_ant as an additional covariate, under temporal (train <2015; validation 2015–2017; external ≥2018), 5°×10° spatial-block and cruise-block validation. Paired model comparisons use a cruise-cluster bootstrap and an equivalence margin of ±4 µmol kg⁻¹.

## 4. Results

### 4.1 The estimator is unbiased; intervals are slightly anticonservative under large cruise offsets
In synthetic data built from the observed structure with known trends (0–1 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹) and random cruise offsets (SD 0–4 µmol kg⁻¹), the mean bias was ≤ 0.012 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (Fig. S1). Bootstrap coverage of nominal 95 % intervals was 90–99 % in 46 of 48 settings. A 200-replicate follow-up of the worst settings (cruise offsets of 4 µmol kg⁻¹) gave 90.5–91 % for the bootstrap and 86–86.5 % for cluster-robust standard errors. We therefore retain the bootstrap and treat intervals that only narrowly exclude a threshold as fragile.

### 4.2 DIC rises at fixed properties with a clear ventilation structure
Observed DIC at fixed θ, S and AOU increases by ≈1.0–1.1 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in the lightest layers of every basin, declining monotonically with density (Fig. 2). Deep layers diverge between basins: 0.29 [0.22, 0.42] µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in Atlantic γⁿ 27.8–28.0 (North Atlantic Deep Water), 0.06–0.07 in the deep Pacific, 0.10 in Southern Ocean bottom water, and indistinguishable from zero in the deep Indian Ocean. The surface value matches the expected equilibrium response of seawater DIC to the atmospheric CO₂ increase (≈ DIC/Revelle × d ln pCO₂/dt ≈ 2000/10 × 2/380 ≈ 1 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹).

### 4.3 Observed and tracer-based rates agree within ±15 % in most layers (H1), but with a systematic excess
Of the 20 basin × layer units with γⁿ ≤ 27.8, 18 support H1 and two contradict it (Pacific γⁿ 27.0–27.5: R = 1.68 [1.40, 2.25]; 27.5–27.8: R = 5.2 [2.9, 13.0], where both rates are small; Fig. 3). The pass/fail verdicts hide a systematic pattern (Fig. 4): in the light layers of all basins except the Atlantic surface (γⁿ < 26), observed DIC rises faster than TRACE C_ant, by δ ≈ +0.10 to +0.17 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (R ≈ 1.13–1.25). Bootstrap intervals of δ exclude zero (δ > 0) in 12 light/intermediate basin × layer units and in the 4 deep Pacific layers; 15 of these 16 also meet the sign-stability rule across sensitivity variants. In the Atlantic surface layer the agreement is close (R = 0.99 [0.89, 1.12]).

### 4.4 The excess is robust to analysis choices but below the systematic-offset detection limit
The sign and approximate size of the light-layer excess are unchanged across all sensitivity variants that use TRACE (Fig. 4, shaded ranges). Leave-one-cruise-out changes β_DIC by at most 0.03 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ outside the sparse Southern Ocean surface layer, and no δ whose interval excludes zero changes sign. Restricting to post-1990 data, when DIC certified reference materials were in general use, leaves the excess unchanged, which argues against an early-calibration artefact. Replacing AOU by phosphate leaves it unchanged or larger. Removing all property conditioning roughly doubles it in the Pacific, showing that conditioning is necessary. However, no |δ| exceeds the conservative offset-equivalent detection limit (0.16–0.19 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹), so a coherent, time-dependent measurement bias of ≈4 µmol kg⁻¹ cannot be formally excluded.

Two smaller deep-layer deviations are robust to every analysis choice but well below the detection limit: Southern Ocean bottom water (γⁿ > 28.2; δ = −0.066 [−0.107, −0.019]; R ≈ 0.6) and the deep Pacific (δ ≈ +0.05). An apparent deficit in deep Atlantic layers (δ ≈ −0.07) shrinks to about −0.01 to −0.02 when pre-1990 data are excluded or phosphate replaces AOU, and is not considered robust.

### 4.5 A DIC-based C_ant estimate sides with the observations (E05)
Over 1994–2007 and at the same sample locations, the eMLR(C*) C_ant change of Gruber et al. (2019) exceeds TRACE by ≈10–35 % in γⁿ < 27.0 in the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific and in the Indo-Pacific intermediate layers (Fig. 6). This comparison does not involve our estimator. Applying the pre-registered decision rule to the 15 layers with a robust excess, 13 indicate "TRACE low" (eMLR closer to observed DIC) and 2 indicate "non-C_ant change or drift" (Indian γⁿ 27.0–27.5; Southern Ocean 26.5–27.0). In Southern Ocean intermediate layers (γⁿ 27.0–27.8) the sign reverses: eMLR(C*) is lower than TRACE (0.46 vs 0.58; 0.26 vs 0.37 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹), while observed DIC agrees with TRACE.

### 4.6 Data quality hardly affects the trends (H4 not supported)
Switching from strict to relaxed QC changes deep-layer β_DIC by at most 0.023 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹, compared with interval half-widths of 0.03–0.10 (0 of 14 deep layers QC-sensitive), even though 15 % of the relaxed sample consists of calculated or non-secondary-QC'd DIC.

### 4.7 Consequences for static empirical DIC models (H3)
Static S–T–AOU regressions trained before 2015 underpredict later DIC in every basin (external bias +4 to +11 µmol kg⁻¹). On the repository's original data, adding a linear time term removes ≥70 % of the holdout bias in 36 of 40 basin × model × split cases (median 83 %) and lowers external RMSE by a median of 2.1 µmol kg⁻¹ (Fig. 5). Under strict QC, the time term meets the criterion in 30 of 40 cases (median 80 % external, 77 % validation). A TRACE C_ant covariate lowers external RMSE more (median −3.4 µmol kg⁻¹) but removes less bias (16 of 40; median 64 %), consistent with §4.3: TRACE accumulates more slowly than observed DIC.

The ranking of functional forms depends on the validation design rather than on the ocean. The rank-1 quadratic, best on the 2015–2017 Atlantic validation set in the original analysis, ranks fourth or fifth in spatial- and cruise-blocked validation, and last or second-to-last on temporal validation under strict QC. With a correct cruise-cluster bootstrap, rank-1, rank-2 and full-quadratic forms are equivalent within ±4 µmol kg⁻¹ in every basin and split, under both the original QC and strict QC (48/48 comparisons). The Indian Ocean temporal-validation and external sets contain only 3 and 4 cruises respectively.

## 5. Discussion

**What the data show.** Fifty years of GLODAP DIC, analysed within fixed locations and at fixed water properties, reveal an accumulation of carbon whose vertical and inter-basin structure closely tracks expectations for anthropogenic CO₂: ≈1 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in surface and mode waters, decreasing with density, with significant accumulation reaching North Atlantic Deep Water but not old Indian deep water. Independent tracer-based estimates (TRACE) reproduce this structure to within ±15 % in 18 of 20 upper and intermediate layers.

**The upper-ocean discrepancy.** Outside the Atlantic surface layer, observed DIC and the DIC-based eMLR(C*) estimate both accumulate ≈10–25 % faster than TRACE in the upper and thermocline layers. Three explanations remain:
1. **TRACE underestimates C_ant accumulation in these waters.** This is plausible: TRACE assumes steady circulation and a fixed TTD shape, and its own validation reports lower inventories than DIC-based mapping below ≈500 m (Carter et al., 2025). Agreement between two DIC-based estimates that use different estimators and conditioning (C* vs AOU) favours this explanation for 13 of 15 layers.
2. **A real natural DIC increase at fixed θ, S, AOU.** Candidates are changes in preformed DIC, air–sea disequilibrium or CaCO₃ dissolution. This would be in tension with the net natural carbon *loss* inferred by Müller et al. (2023), unless compensated elsewhere.
3. **Residual measurement drift.** It cannot be excluded at the 4 µmol kg⁻¹ level, but it is not supported by the post-1990 test.

Because eMLR(C*) is itself derived from GLODAP DIC, its agreement with our trends is not independent confirmation. The finding is best stated as a DIC-versus-tracer discrepancy, robust to analysis choices, which favours a low bias in TTD-based rates in the upper ocean outside the Southern Ocean.

**Southern Ocean.** The pattern reverses in Southern Ocean intermediate layers, where eMLR(C*) is below TRACE and observed DIC agrees with TRACE. In bottom water, observed DIC accumulates ≈40 % more slowly than TRACE (below the detection limit). Both are consistent with Steinfeldt et al. (2024), who found the largest departures from steady state in the Southern Ocean and subpolar North Atlantic (H2 partly supported). AOU conditioning is a known weakness here (O₂ disequilibrium at deep-water formation; Ito et al., 2004), although phosphate conditioning gave the same sign.

**Implications for empirical DIC models.** Static regressions of DIC on hydrography are not temporally transferable. Their holdout errors are dominated by a predictable anthropogenic signal of ≈0.3–0.4 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (depth-averaged), and model rankings depend on the validation design. Conclusions about functional form, such as "one-dimensional" quadratic curvature, should therefore not be drawn from temporal holdouts without modelling the trend, and differences below DIC measurement consistency (~4 µmol kg⁻¹) are not meaningful. Established tools (ESPER, CANYON-B, the mapped GLODAPv2) already include time or C_ant adjustments; our results quantify why this matters.

## 6. Limitations
* **Detection limit.** No deviation exceeds the offset-equivalent detection limit; the upper-ocean excess (2.5–4 µmol kg⁻¹ over the record) is comparable to GLODAP's adjustment threshold.
* **Independence.** eMLR(C*) uses the same GLODAP DIC. TRACE was evaluated with default settings only (no disequilibrium or TTD-shape sensitivity).
* **Interval coverage.** Bootstrap intervals cover ≈91 % rather than 95 % under large cruise offsets.
* **Single linear trend.** We fit one linear trend per layer over 1972–2021. Under transient steady state the accumulation rate increases over time, and sampling eras differ between basins, which makes R period-dependent. The windowed analysis (1989–2012) only partly addresses this.
* **AOU conditioning.** AOU is not true oxygen utilisation in Southern Ocean source waters.
* **Coverage.** Cell inclusion favours repeat sections; marginal seas and the Arctic are excluded; the Indian Ocean has few cruises.
* **Not causal.** The analysis is observational and associational. Attribution of δ to TRACE bias, natural carbon change or measurement drift is inferential, not causal.

## 7. Conclusions
1. At fixed water properties and within fixed locations, GLODAP DIC increased by ≈1 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹ in light layers, decreasing with density and basin age, consistent in structure with anthropogenic CO₂ uptake.
2. TRACE reproduces these rates within ±15 % in 18 of 20 upper and intermediate layers, but observed DIC (and eMLR(C*)) accumulate systematically faster than TRACE in the upper ocean outside the Southern Ocean, by ≈0.1–0.17 µmol kg⁻¹ yr⁻¹. The excess is robust to analysis choices but below a conservative measurement-drift detection limit.
3. Static DIC regressions on S, T and AOU are confounded by this signal. A time or C_ant covariate removes most of their temporal bias, and their apparent model rankings depend on the validation design.
